title: Challenging People to Think
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece describes a specific interrogative technique rather than a general exhortation to think harder. It starts from the observation that people gravitate toward confirming existing beliefs and toward company that validates them, and positions the leader's job as asking for one more step beyond what is known or assumed to be known. The method has two parts. First, ask people for their so-called facts, the propositions they treat as settled, then test them: how solid are they, why do others disagree, and why do they matter. Second, and this is where the essay distinguishes itself, ask the person to manufacture the reasons someone holding the contrary view might give. It draws a sharp line between this and playing devil's advocate, which merely acknowledges an opposing position; the demand here is to generate the opposing case, on the grounds that doing so exposes the weaknesses in one's own reasoning and improves one's ability to answer objections later. The closing formulation states the aim precisely: not to change a person's mind, but to get their mind to embrace change.
points: The technique is specified in two steps, surfacing the propositions someone treats as settled, then asking how solid they are, why others disagree and why they matter.
The distinctive demand is to manufacture the opposing case rather than acknowledge it, which the piece explicitly separates from playing devil's advocate.
The justification is diagnostic: constructing the counter-argument is what reveals the weaknesses in one's own reasoning, and incidentally prepares a better answer to future objections.
The starting observation is that most people are in an echo chamber by default, seeking others who confirm rather than test their views.
The stated aim is precise and worth keeping, not to change a person's mind but to get their mind to embrace change.
quotes: They challenge others to stretch their views beyond what is comfortable and commonplace.
People naturally gravitate toward confirming their existing beliefs and opinions, and they seek out others to validate their views.
In many cases, statements team members adhere to are more opinions than indisputable facts.
Asking team members to take the other side of their opinion and generate a few reasons or arguments that someone who holds a contrasting view might believe gets the wheel turning.
This is not a devil’s advocate mission to simply acknowledge the opposing view. The ask here is to manufacture the reasons for any disagreement.
By taking on the opposing perspective, team members better learn the weaknesses in their own reasoning.
The idea is not to change a person’s mind. It is to get a person’s mind to embrace change.
